title: Sea state, swell and wind against tide
summary: How waves grow, swell versus wind sea, wave statistics, and why wind against tide turns a sea dangerous.

segments.heading: Strength, fetch and duration
paragraphs: Wind waves grow with wind strength, fetch (the distance of open water the wind blows across) and duration (how long it has blown). The smallest of the three limits the sea. A gale blowing offshore leaves a short fetch and a modest sea near the coast; the same gale with hundreds of miles of fetch builds a large, fully developed sea.

Forecast wave heights are usually significant wave heights: the mean of the highest third. Among a thousand waves, expect one around 1.9 times the significant height. Plan for the bigger waves, not the average.
keyPoints: Strength, fetch and duration together set the wave height.
Significant height is the mean of the highest third.
Occasional waves nearly twice that height.

segments.heading: Swell versus wind sea
paragraphs: Swell is long-period energy that has left the generating area. It travels far and fast and can arrive ahead of a storm, a valuable early warning. Wind waves are shorter, steeper and aligned with the local wind.

When swell and wind sea come from different directions, the sea becomes confused and crests can combine into steep, breaking peaks. Swell running into shallow water or against a current steepens dangerously, and can break across harbour bars.

lessons.title: Wind against tide and shallow water

segments.heading: Why it steepens
paragraphs: When the wind blows against the tidal stream, the waves are effectively compressed: the wavelength shortens while height increases, so the sea becomes steep and breaks. A Force 5 against a 3-knot stream can raise a sea far steeper than a Force 5 normally produces. When the tide turns to run with the wind, the same sea lengthens and eases.
The effect is worst at headlands, over shoals and in tidal races and overfalls. Plan to pass such places at slack water or with wind and tide together.
keyPoints: Wind against tide: shorter, steeper, breaking waves.
Worst at headlands, races, overfalls and over shoals.
Time passages for slack water or wind with tide.

segments.heading: Sea state terms
paragraphs: Forecasts describe sea state by significant height: smooth (up to 0.5 m), slight (0.5 to 1.25 m), moderate (1.25 to 2.5 m), rough (2.5 to 4 m), very rough (4 to 6 m), high (6 to 9 m), very high (9 to 14 m) and phenomenal (over 14 m).
Use the Beaufort descriptions to cross-check observed wind against the sea: white horses begin around Force 4, foam streaks at Force 7, and spindrift at Force 8.

segments.heading: Races, overfalls and bars
paragraphs: Tidal races form where a strong stream is squeezed round a headland or over an uneven bottom; overfalls are the steep, breaking seas this produces. Portland Bill, St Alban's Head and the Alderney Race are well-known examples. With wind against the stream they can be dangerous even in moderate winds, and a swell running in makes them worse.

Harbour bars break when an onshore swell meets shallow water, often worst on the ebb when the outgoing stream steepens the waves. Many bars are safest on the flood near high water, but some have their own windows, strong flood streams or swell limits. Use the pilot book, local notices and the harbour authority, check your under-keel clearance, watch the bar before committing, and do not cross if it is breaking. Keep well off a race or take the recognised inshore passage at the right time.
keyPoints: Races and overfalls: strong stream over headlands and uneven ground.
Bars are often worst on the ebb with onshore swell.
Follow local pilotage; never cross a breaking bar.

segments.heading: Significant height and the bigger waves
paragraphs: Wave forecasts and buoy reports give the significant wave height: the average height of the highest third of the waves, close to what an experienced observer would estimate. Many waves are lower, and some are much higher.

Over a few hours, expect occasional individual waves of about twice the significant height, and rarely more. A forecast of 2 m can therefore bring the odd wave of 4 m or so, and that is the wave that fills a cockpit or knocks a boat down.
keyPoints: Significant height: mean of the highest third.
Expect occasional waves of about twice that height, rarely more.
Plan for the big wave, not the average.

segments.heading: Period, swell and combined seas
paragraphs: Wave period matters as much as height. In deep water the wavelength in metres is roughly 1.56 times the period squared: a 5-second sea is about 40 m long, a 12-second swell about 225 m. A 2 m wave at 5 seconds is short and steep and may break; the same height at 12 seconds is a long, gentle swell.

Forecasts may give wind sea and swell separately, each with its own height, period and direction, or a combined figure. When swell and wind sea come from different directions the result is a confused cross sea, which is uncomfortable and harder to steer through. Two forecasts with the same height can therefore mean very different conditions.
keyPoints: Short period plus height means steep, breaking seas.
Read wind sea and swell separately: height, period, direction.
Cross seas from two directions are confused and tiring.

questions.prompt: A north-easterly Force 7 has blown for 12 hours. Where will the sea be smallest?
options: Close under a coast to the north-east, where the wind blows off the land
Over a shallow bank 50 miles offshore
optionExplanations: Correct: short fetch means little room for waves to build.
Long fetch means a bigger sea.
Unlimited fetch.
Shallow water steepens the waves that arrive.
questions.explanation: Fetch limits the waves: an offshore wind close under the weather shore gives the flattest water.

questions.prompt: The forecast significant wave height is 2.5 m. Roughly how high might the occasional largest wave be, in metres? (Use 1.9 times.)
questions.explanation: 2.5 × 1.9 ≈ 4.75 m. Prepare boat and crew for occasional waves of that size.

questions.context: You plan to round a headland with a known tidal race. Wind: west-south-west Force 5. The tidal stream off the headland runs west at up to 3 knots from 10:00 to 16:00 and east from 16:00 to 22:00.
questions.explanation: Pass with wind and tide together, or at slack, to avoid steep breaking seas in the race.

steps.prompt: During which period is the wind against the tide?
optionExplanations: Correct: a west-south-westerly wind blows towards the east-north-east, against a westgoing stream.
The eastgoing stream runs with the wind.
There is an opposing period.
The stream reverses.
steps.explanation: A west-south-west wind blows towards the east; a westgoing stream opposes it.

steps.prompt: When should you plan to pass the race?
options: Around 16:00 at slack, or soon after as the eastgoing stream begins
At 10:00 as the westgoing stream begins
optionExplanations: Maximum wind-against-tide: worst sea.
Correct: slack, then wind and tide together.
Force 5 against 3 knots can feel like Force 7 in a race.
The stream is building against the wind.
steps.explanation: Slack water or a fair stream with the wind gives the easiest sea through a race.

questions.prompt: A long, low swell starts arriving from the south-west on a calm, clear day. What might it indicate?
optionExplanations: Swell always has a source.
Correct: swell can arrive well ahead of the wind.
Unrelated.
Unrelated.
questions.explanation: Swell travels faster than most storms; a new, growing swell can be the first sign of approaching bad weather.

questions.prompt: Put these sea-state terms in order of increasing wave height.
questions.explanation: Smooth, slight, moderate, rough, very rough (then high, very high, phenomenal).

questions.prompt: At about which Beaufort force do white horses become widespread?
optionExplanations: Force 2 has small wavelets only.
Correct: fairly frequent white horses at Force 4.
At Force 7 foam is blown in streaks.
Force 9 has dense foam and spray.
questions.explanation: White horses appear at Force 3 and become fairly frequent at Force 4.

questions.prompt: Which conditions make a harbour bar dangerous to cross? Select all that apply.
options: Ebb tide running out against the swell
optionExplanations: Correct.
Correct: the ebb steepens and breaks the swell.
This is the safest time.
Correct.
Generally the easiest combination.
questions.explanation: Swell, onshore wind and an ebb running against them make bars break; cross near high water slack in quiet conditions.

questions.prompt: What does a forecast wave height usually refer to?
options: The significant wave height: mean of the highest third
optionExplanations: Individual maxima are higher.
The average is lower than significant height.
Correct.
It includes both wind sea and swell unless stated.
questions.explanation: Significant wave height approximates what an observer would estimate; occasional waves are much larger.

questions.prompt: A forecast gives a significant wave height of 2 m. What is the largest individual wave you should prepare for over several hours?
optionExplanations: Many waves are lower, but that is not the risk.
That is the significant height, not the largest wave.
Correct: occasional waves near twice the significant height.
Far beyond what a 2 m sea produces.
questions.explanation: Plan for occasional waves of about twice the significant height.

questions.prompt: Two seas are both 2 m high. Which is the more dangerous for a small yacht?
options: It depends only on wind strength
optionExplanations: Correct: about 40 m long, steep and likely to break.
About 225 m long: a long, gentle swell.
Period changes steepness.
Period and height together set steepness.
questions.explanation: A short period means short, steep waves; the same height at a long period is gentle swell.

questions.prompt: You plan to enter a harbour over a bar with a moderate onshore swell. When should you cross?
options: On the flood, near high water
At low water, when the bar is visible
Any time, if the engine is reliable
optionExplanations: The ebb steepens the swell: worst time.
Correct: most depth and the stream with the swell.
Least depth: waves break most readily.
Engine reliability does not stop breaking seas.
questions.explanation: Generally cross on the flood near high water, subject to local pilotage advice, and not at all if the bar is breaking.
